utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39 & 40-PT, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik and Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. My name is Mark Harmon. Appearing with me today to my right is Mr. Alan Tieger and, to his right, Mr. Thomas Hannis; and to my left is the case manager, Ms. Carmela Annink-Javier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Deyan Brashich with Nikola Kostich for the Krajisnik defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Eugene O'Sullivan and Peter Murphy appearing on behalf of Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We have in front of us the motion for relief in relation to the trial of this case. We have the motions from both sides which we've read -- from all sides, I should say, which we've read. We will hear some argument, additional argument, on that matter. We would also wish to hear what progress has been made on the translation project and generally as to the progress in getting this case ready for trial. We have only the courtroom -- I'm sorry we started late. It was because the previous case ran over. We have the courtroom for an hour and a quarter or so. We will then have to vacate it for another case to come in. So within those parameters, of course, we are ready to hear submissions. We will begin with the motion, as I said, on behalf of the Plavsic Defence, to exclude evidence and limit the scope of the trial. Mr. Murphy, you're going to address that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I think the Court is aware that one of the grounds originally put forward in the motion related to the apparent extension of the case to Croatia, and I believe that the Trial Chamber has been made aware that the parties were able to resolve that question by agreement and that it is not before the Court today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we've heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the remaining grounds or requests for relief have only one goal as far as the Plavsic Defence is concerned, and that is the goal of securing a fair trial for these accused in accordance with the timetable that the Trial Chamber has in mind, which currently calls for the Defence pre-trial briefs to be filed no later than the 1st of September of this year and that trial should thereafter proceed perhaps in October or November, depending upon availability of the Judges and so on. The relief that we are seeking is not relief of our own invention. It is, in fact, relief that has been envisaged by the Trial Chamber, specifically the Pre-Trial Judge, for many months now. We have sought, I think somewhat diligently, to cooperate with the Prosecution, with the Tribunal in resolving the problems in this case. I cite by way of example the fact that it was the Plavsic Defence which identified and I think recruited the 19 language assistants who are presently staffing the Novi Sad pilot translation project. But as Judge May observed on an earlier occasion, there is an institutional problem which can be described as intractable regarding translation. And, Your Honours, the time has come, in our submission, when that question must now be squarely faced. And the issue perhaps raised by this motion is who is going to suffer because of the problems caused by this institutional condition? There is a danger, if nothing is done, that it will be the accused who suffer through not having proper access to the evidence which they need, firstly to evaluate the case and prepare the pre-trial brief and then to enjoy a fair trial as mandated by Articles 20 and 21 of the Statute. I think that the Trial Chamber, the Pre-Trial Judge, has made it clear in the past to the Prosecution that in the face of this problem, it should have been for the Prosecution to tailor its case to the available resources. In our motion, we have set out the statistics, the figures, as it were, regarding the number of documents, the number of untranslated documents, and judging by the response filed by the Prosecution, these figures are not in dispute. And for all the persuasion that the Trial Court has offered to the Prosecution, there has been no evidence so far that the scale of the case has been reduced at all. Indeed, on the contrary, it has increased. Now, the Prosecution has, and I say this not by way of criticism but in grudging admiration to my learned friends on that side of the case, woven a quite remarkable illusion about the documents. Back in April of 2001, at the Status Conference, we were painted the picture of an archive of some 2.7 million documents which the Prosecution had. And I think the impression was given that they were going through this archive of 2.7 million documents to determine how many of those might be relevant. Perhaps this presupposes that in all the years preceding the indictment of these accused there had been no initial investigation of the matter which might have revealed which of these documents was relevant. But we have this picture of the Prosecution sailing, as it were, through uncharted waters, navigating their way through their own basement, like Jason in pursuit of the Golden Fleece, to try to determine which of these 2.7 million documents are necessary. But then, at the next Status Conference on the 23rd of May, the Prosecution returned with remarkable news. They said: We've narrowed the field. We've now identified 104.000 of those documents as provisionally relevant. Now, Your Honours, when one looks at 2.7 million and when one looks at 104.000, the ultimate number of 11.000 seems rather small. But we would submit that that's not really the way to look at it. Looking back, again, we set out the history in our motion - I need not repeat it - but looking back, there was a time when we were talking in terms of 800 core documents and where there was an optimistic projection, I think by the Court, of 2.000 being about right. And what has actually happened has not been a retreat from 2.7 million documents or 104.000 documents, it's been a steady advance from 800 core to perhaps 2.000 total, to the present-day situation of more than 11.000. I don't want to multiply figures, I just would, however, like to draw the Court's attention to a fact that we would anyway talk about in the Status Conference which we didn't have at the time of filing the motion, which is that now that we've got the pre-trial brief, we estimate - and I do say estimate, it may be a little off one way or the other - but approximately 1.100 documents are referred to in that brief. In one portion of it that we have analysed with some care, the general section, in which they talk about the joint criminal enterprise and the general theory of the case, there are 547 documents of which roughly a third have been disclosed to us only in B/C/S. And as for the much-vaunted core documents, there are now over 2.400 of those, and yet in the same passage of the pre-trial brief, only 314 are cited. And yet the Defence has been served with more than 11.000, some 48 per cent of which are available to us only in B/C/S. Now, I mention these facts to -- because it's our contention that to leave the case in that position, with the trial looming in November, is unfair by anybody's standards. I would like, if I may, Your Honour, to address one or two of the matters raised by the Prosecution in its response to our motion. Firstly, the Prosecution says, "Well, the Defence has been given sufficient notice of what the case is about through the indictment and through the pre-trial brief." I'm sure the Trial Chamber will recall that when the Prosecution moved to amend the consolidated indictment, we objected to that and we said that it did not give us specifics. The Trial Chamber was against us on that point, but it did point out that we could expect to have a full statement of the case linking the allegations in the indictment with the evidence at the time when the pre-trial brief was filed. Now, I suppose a question arises when is a pre-trial brief not a pre-trial brief? If extrapolating, it may well be that one-third of the documents, approximately, which are cited to in the brief are only in B/C/S, can it be said that we've really been given access to that evidence? The Prosecution argues further that, "Well, the Defence only has to put forward a general statement of the defence. They don't have to go into a great deal of detail." Be that as it may, we on the Defence side regard the Defence pre-trial brief as a very important document. It is our intention to tell the Court as far as we can and in as much detail as we can exactly what we dispute in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, why we dispute it, and to put forward a statement of Mrs. Plavsic's defence. We cannot do that without access to the evidence. The Prosecution next argues and I quote the language of their response, "that an attempt to impose a blanket exclusion of evidence is premature, arbitrary and not justified." Let's look at that. Premature. If not now, when? We have a pre-trial brief due on the 1st of September. We're going to trial in just a few months. Arbitrary. Well, Your Honour, we're asking for relief that the Pre-Trial Judge himself suggested might have to be given. We don't consider that to be arbitrary; in fact, we consider it to be necessary. And thirdly, not justified. Well, what we have here is a situation where the Defence has such a large number of documents available only in B/C/S, and such a large number of documents, frankly, that don't appear to be worthy of being cited in the pre-trial brief, that we are effectively being inundated with paper. Just to take one other point which is perhaps peripheral but deserves mention, the Plavsic Defence has initiated reciprocal discovery under Rule 67, and without access to the evidence, it may well be that there are requests for further discovery that we should be making that we cannot make at this time simply because we really don't know how these other documents relate to the case as a whole. The Prosecution says, "Well, it's not matter for this Trial Chamber anyway, because the Trial Chamber which tries the case should rule on the exclusion of evidence." Apparently the Prosecution do not feel, however, that the same principle applies to motions to admit evidence under Rule 92 bis, which they have already made and will be making further motions, nor do they feel, apparently, that it applies to motions for judicial notice. We have received a total of over 1.300 alleged adjudicated facts which the Prosecution intends to ask this Trial Chamber apparently to take judicial notice. We believe that the law and the practice in this Tribunal strongly suggests that it is indeed a function of this Trial Chamber to make rulings which will get the case in a position to be tried fairly. The Prosecution then argues that they have complied with the Rules because the Rules only require that we be given copies of the exhibits, it does not require that we be given them in English. That can be done at the time of trial. Your Honours, the Rules, of course, must be followed, but equally, the Rules must take second place to the basic principles of fairness under Articles 20 and 21. What I'm being told by the Prosecution, apparently, is that I should take 4.000 or 5.000 documents to Mrs. Plavsic, a lady now approaching her 72nd birthday, who resides in Belgrade under the order of the court, and ask her to read through these documents and tell me what they say. Now, Mrs. Plavsic's English is not bad. It's good for most conversational purposes. But we are talking here about documents that in many cases are very technical, have legal significance, and it's quite impossible to ask Mrs. Plavsic to read through them and make judgements of that kind which would be necessarily involved. Essentially what the Prosecution is saying is that Mrs. Plavsic is unrepresented because she doesn't have the effective assistance of counsel. Your Honour, these are not the Prosecution's problems. I accept this. What we have here is an institutional problem, and the question is: Who must suffer because of it? I would respectfully suggest to the Court that at this point there are three possible scenarios. One, which I hope that we would all reject, is that the trial would proceed on an unfair basis. The second is that the Trial Chamber should do what has been suggested in the past and scale this case down to manageable proportions so that we can be ready for trial in the fall. The third, which I suspect will not be very palatable to the Trial Chamber but I must raise it, is that if that is not done, then the accused must be given adequate time to prepare the case. And when I say "adequate," unfortunately I have to mean in this context a substantial amount of time to go through so many documents, so many of which have not been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What would your idea be of that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: If the case remains in the posture of 11.000 plus documents -- and incidentally, Your Honour, we're still receiving them. We got 84 more documents this week, of I would about 40 per cent were in B/C/S. If that remains the case, we -- I don't see that anything less than six months would be possible to the date when we can file a pre-trial brief. Now, we are anxious to comply with the Court's guideline. This is not said to occasion delay, but the issue here is one of fundamental fairness. Unless the Court has any questions further, I will defer any further matters until the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help us, Mr. Murphy, on how the translation is going at the moment? Are you in a position to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I can. I suspect Mr. Tieger knows a little bit more about that than I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And your estimate of six months would hinge on the pace at which you get the translations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, what's happening at the moment, and I understand that Mr. Tieger will correct me if I'm wrong, but we have the pilot translation project operating in Novi Sad, and what happens is the Prosecution supplies draft translations, they are then sent to Novi Sad and worked on by a group of 19 language assistants. These are not fully-qualified interpreters because this scheme, frankly, was set up not to deal with important documents but to deal with relatively less important ones which we could make do with the rough translations. When they come back from Novi Sad, we have to review them, the Krajisnik Defence has to review them, the Prosecution reviews them, and then if everybody is happy, we have an agreed translation. And in fairness, it's working quite well, but the problem is only so much material can be sent at one time. We had a very useful meeting with the Prosecution yesterday at which they invited us to prioritise the documents that we would like to send, and we said in response to that, "Well, first of all, please send everything that's in the pre-trial brief that's in B/C/S. Secondly, please send the core documents." They agreed to do that and that will help tremendously. Even allowing for that, it's difficult to think that this process could really be accomplished much before the beginning of September. In my view. Mr. Tieger may differ from that. And as I understand it, Your Honour, that's really the state of play as regards the translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Good morning -- or good afternoon, Your Honour. The Krajisnik Defence has joined in the motion. However, with regard to the relief that we seek, we differ slightly with the Plavsic Defence. Mr. Murphy made it very clear that the Defence believes that there are three options open to the Court. While we join with option number one and two, we do not join in the extension of time which is option number three. Mrs. Plavsic is living in Belgrade and has been living in Belgrade for quite some time. My client, since April of 2000, has been living in Scheveningen and not in a hotel. I believe that the proper relief is that any and all documents that are not referred to in the pre-trial brief should be excluded and we should go forward with the trial in October. Just a final point, Your Honour, and a thought came to me. If it's not in the pre-trial brief, then it really is not that relevant. And if we're going to rely on the specificity of the pre-trial brief, then that's it; exclude everything else. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, there are some documents in the pre-trial brief not translated. In terms of your submission, I understand you then to say that you would await the translation of those, they being in the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: If I understand the conversation between Mr. Tieger and Mr. Murphy of yesterday afternoon, the documents in the pre-trial brief are going to be sent to Novi Sad I believe this afternoon. That's my understanding. The only other comment that I can make, Your Honour, is that in view of the passage of legislation in Yugoslavia and in light of the fact that one individual was in fact arrested in Yugoslavia under the new legislation, perhaps this Court, in giving my client Mr. Krajisnik a fair trial, would revisit its view on provisional release and allow him not to go back to Bosnia, which I believe there is some feeling on the part of the Court that that particular entity has not fully complied, but we now have Yugoslavia complying, Mrs. Plavsic living, and Mr. Krajisnik agreeing to confine himself to a city or a small geographic locality within Yugoslavia and not Bosnia. Should the Court revisit its decision, all of the warranties and undertakings that I have made on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik, together with this new legislation in place and enforceable, because do not forget that the person who was arrested, the first person who was arrested, was a Serb from Bosnia, which is the same situation Mr. Krajisnik would find himself in. And of course, Mr. Krajisnik is much more visible an individual than this new accused. Should the Court revisit its decision, I would then be able to join Mr. Murphy and the Plavsic Defence and allow the Prosecution to fully comply with its obligations under the Rules, then there would not be the time constraint and it would almost be a calendaring matter by stipulation between the parties. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the impulse behind the motion, as I have read it, is an attempt to reduce this case. And let me begin my remarks by saying that on the last -- at the last Status Conference, the 10th of May, I addressed the Prosecutor's numerous attempts to attempt to reduce this case by using the innovative Rules that have been made available to both parties, and specifically I addressed the issue of 92 bis, adjudicated facts, expert reports under 94 bis. And as I have mentioned, just to cite one example, in the issue of adjudicated facts where we had submitted the first part of the adjudicated facts to the Defence over 20 months ago, I think the Court should revisit the remarks made at the Status Conference by the Prosecutor, and we'll see that we have made every effort for a long period of time through this litigation to reduce this case. The Defence has chosen to focus on one matter, that is the matter that is an institutional problem and that is translations, to suggest that the Prosecutor has not been conscientious in trying to reduce this case in size and in scope. I would also like to point out the fact that these cases are not static, that the developments from the time this case was indicted that have resulted in part for the augmentation of exhibits is a result of events in the former Yugoslavia. The opening of the former Yugoslavia and the cooperation of the Belgrade authorities have created additional documents. The greater cooperation of the Republika Srpska has created and resulted in additional documents. But now, those are events that have impacted on why the exhibit list has been augmented. But I want to address really directly the issue that is raised in this motion, and that is the application by the Defence to have this Trial Chamber exclude relevant evidence and relevant witnesses from being heard by another Chamber that will in fact and indeed hear this case. Now, the Defence contends in its motion that these Draconian measures are necessary in order for it to prepare its pre-trial brief and to prepare for trial. Let me address at the outset the requirements under Rule 65 ter (F) which are the requirements that the Defence now finds itself having to deal with in respect of its pre-trial brief. Under Rule 65 ter (F), the Defence is required to address the factual and legal issues in the case and in general terms identify the nature of the Defence and identify matters that were in the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief with which it takes issue, and where it takes issue, to state why it takes issue. That's the requirement that the Defence has in preparing a pre-trial brief that is due in three months. Now, it is our position, Your Honours, that while they have difficulties with the translation issue, as does most everybody who is involved in this litigation in this institution, those issues have been addressed and will be addressed and will put them in a position, in a proper position, to prepare a pre-trial brief as required by Rule 65 ter (F). And I say that because, one, they have received to date the amended consolidated indictment, which indictment set forth the material facts as to each of the counts in the -- of the charges. That indictment was found to be sufficient by Your Honours and subsequently by an Appeals Chamber in the denial of the Defence application for leave to appeal. Virtually all of the witness statements have been provided to the accused's counsel in English. All of the exhibits that are presently intended to be used at trial have been provided to the Defence, albeit there are significant problems that relate to the translations, which I will address shortly. The Defence was provided with a provisional pre-trial brief nine months ago, August 31st of 2001, in which the provisional pre-trial brief identified the case that the Defence had to answer, included summaries of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. each of the witnesses the Prosecutor intended to call, listed exhibits that the Prosecutor intended to present during the course of the proceedings. And lastly, Your Honours, one month ago, four weeks ago, the Prosecutor filed a final pre-trial brief. That was filed on the 2nd of May, 2002, and that list contained, again, the summaries of each of the witnesses intended to be called by the Prosecutor, the summary of their proposed testimonies, and a list of exhibits. So it is our submission, Your Honours, based on what the Defence has been presented, they have been clearly apprised of the nature of the case they have to answer and they are in a position and will be in a position on September the 1st to be able to state in general terms the nature of their respective defences, why they -- what they take issue with in our pre-trial brief, and why they do so. Now, I'd like to turn to the motion itself, because the motion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, what if the material which is not before them now is new material, new and important material requiring an answer from them?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If -- of course. Of course the Rules provide for both parties, on receipt of new and additional information, to file an application with the Trial Chamber, making a request for the permission to use that evidence, and we intend to do so as the trial proceeds. It has -- it is a practice that has been accepted in the course of litigation in this case and indeed in the Krstic case in which I was one of the Prosecutors. After the case closed, both parties had rested, an application was made for the receipt of newly-discovered and important evidence, and that motion was granted. So, yes, Judge Robinson, I anticipate that there will be occasions when additional and new evidence comes to our attention that is important and relevant and we will make a suitable application. But that applies to both parties and both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It does have the inconvenience of lengthening the trial. If that material were available now, it could be dealt with in their pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Of course. If we had it and it was relevant, we would have identified it. But I am addressing a situation where we don't have it in our possession and we come across it during the course of the trial. Now, it may also have the effect of reducing the length of the trial, given the significance of the piece of evidence or the witness that comes forward but I'm not in a position to address future events. I can just outline and present possibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Now, the four bases that the Defence has identified as underpinning their request to ask you to impose these rather extraordinary measures are the following: First of all, the document crisis. The second is the experts. The third is the Croatian issue that has been withdrawn, and lastly, events that relate to the 31st of December, 1992, beyond that particular date. And I will address each one of these issues in order. If I could turn first of all to the document crisis. The relief that has been sought there is to preclude from adducing at trial any document in B/C/S which hasn't been translated into English by the 2nd of May. Now, the translation problem that we are confronting in this case is not unique. It is an institutional problem and it was recognised as such in the Galic case, an Appeal Court recognised it as a "constant problem within the Tribunal." And I refer Your Honours to the decision on the application by the Prosecution for leave to appeal in Galic, dated the 14th of December, 2001. Now, this situation that confronts us is not a situation where the Prosecutor has been acting intentionally or maliciously. Indeed, as Mr. Murphy has said, the parties have acted together in cooperation, attempting to resolve the problems. And the pilot project conceived by Mr. Tieger in cooperation -- and implemented in cooperation with the Plavsic Defence in identifying the translators required for that is one such innovation. The statistics that I'll turn to now and I'll be addressing really I bring to your attention because, as the Defence has said on page 12 of their motion, and I quote: "The translation rate will not make a large enough dent in the backlog of untranslated documents and certainly not make a large enough dent in it within the time frame which the Trial Chamber has established for both the pre-trial date and the trial itself." They raised similar concerns at the 65 ter conference on the 19th of April, and we responded to them saying we were undertaking steps to ameliorate the problem. On the 10th of May, at the Status Conference, Mr. Tieger advised Your Honours that the project had been augmented substantially and the capacity of the project to translate documents had resulted in the product going from several hundred pages a month to several thousand pages a month. Now, when Mr. Tieger raised that issue at the 10th of May Status Conference, Mr. Pavich, my esteemed colleague from the Defence, responded, and I will quote him. He said: "It would be impossible for us to make the commitments --" he's referring to meeting the pre-trial brief schedule and the trial date -- "unless we can determine that this proposal that we've heard for the first time to day is in fact a realistic proposal. Will the institution be able to go from translating less than a hundred pages a month to several thousand pages a month? Perhaps a status conference in the next two or three weeks will enable us to assess and put us in a position where we can be more realistic -- give a more realistic response to the Court." That's found at page 260 of the transcript. And that's the reason that we're here today, to advise Your Honours of the status of the translation project and the pilot project, in part. Therefore, I am pleased to give you the information relating to the progress that has been made. On the 17th of May, we submitted for Defence review 867 pages of documents. Today we're submitting approximately another 1.500 pages of documents to the Defence. All of this was achieved with a new regime that wasn't fully in place until the last two weeks of this month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are documents which are being translated by the pilot project.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct. Now, we are, in addition, we're augmenting I've been informed, the pilot project -- the capacity of the pilot project to translate documents will be augmented further in June by an additional 20 per cent, and that will result, by our best estimates, of translations at the rate of 4.000 pages per month. Now, in addition to the increased rate of translations that is being achieved, we are, in a parallel effort, deselecting documents from the exhibit list. As a result of that effort to date, we have deselected 2.950 pages of documents that no longer need translation. That deselection process is continuing and will continue throughout this process. Now, in light of this regime, we calculated that all of the core documents would be translated by the end of June, and all of the documents presently on the list would be translated by the beginning of October with one exception, and that one exception Your Honours are fully aware of. It is the untranslated forensic reports which were the subject of a discussion with Your Honours on the 10th of May Status Conference. And those reports, incidentally, are reports for which the defendant is aware of the contents because the Registrar appointed a joint forensic -- joint Defence forensic expert who has reviewed the untranslated forensic reports and has given the Defence advice that resulted in their not accepting any of the Rule 94 bis expert forensic reports. Now, I said to Your Honours that we had calculated that all of the core documents would be translated by the end of June. Yesterday, we met with Mr. Murphy and Mr. O'Sullivan in an effort to continue trying to find how best to assist them to overcome this translation crisis. We suggested to them that if they prioritised the documents they wanted translated, we would make sure those documents went to the front of the queue. Mr. O'Sullivan and Mr. Murphy informed us that they did establish a priority list. They wanted the documents that were in the pre-trial brief that were untranslated to go to the front of the queue. Next, they wanted the core documents next in order, and lastly, the remaining documents. We agreed to that. Now, we also went back and did the mathematics of that, and there are apparently a total of 1.016 documents in the pre-trial brief, 347 of which need translation. Now, these documents, Your Honours, will be translated by the end of June. In addition, by, we estimate, next Wednesday but no later than next Friday, we will provide the Defence with comprehensive -- in some respects comprehensive summaries of the untranslated 347 documents that appear in the footnotes. It is our submission, Your Honour, that the Defence request to exclude untranslated documents should be rejected. I do say, and I will repeat today I said in the filing we made that the request is premature. We have in good faith attempted to overcome the institutional problem that has confronted us in this particular case and, through innovative efforts, we have achieved a substantial success in that regard. In addition, Your Honours, there are alternatives to the wholesale exclusion of evidence, and I will give you an example of one such type of innovation, suggestion that could be made; and that is if there is indeed a document that is not translated by the time the case comes to trial, there could be a time restriction on when that document could be led in evidence. For example, there could be a restriction that an untranslated document could not be led into evidence for a period of ten days minimum until it's been finally translated and given to the Defence. I'm not advocating that now because I've suggested that all of the documents will be completely translated by the beginning of October. So it is our position, Your Honours, that Your Honours should reject the application to exclude all of the documents that have not been translated by the 2nd of May. Now, the second prong of the argument why this case -- why this motion should result in a diminution of the Prosecutor's evidence is under the chapeau of the unlisted experts. And there are two prongs to that particular argument. The first prong is we should be precluded from calling at trial any witness not listed by name or pseudonym in the list of witnesses that we supplied with our pre-trial brief. And the second form of relief sought under that chapeau is that we should be precluded from calling any expert witnesses whose expert report was not disclosed by the 2nd of May. Now, if I turn to the first prong, that is exclude from -- prevent the Prosecutor from calling at trial any witness not listed by name in our pre-trial brief, it is our submission, Your Honour, that under Article 22 and Rules 69 and 75, and under exceptional circumstances, delayed disclosure of identities of witnesses is permissible. Therefore, we would request that that part of their motion be rejected. As to the second prong of this particular argument, that is to reduce the scale of the case by excluding any expert whose report wasn't filed by the 2nd of May, 2002, again this request is premature. What this request is is a request to Your Honours to prevent the Trial Chamber that's going to hear this case from hearing any expert testimony whatsoever other than forensic evidence. In other words, they're asking you to prevent the Trial Chamber in -- that will actually hear case from hearing experts on the topic of the destruction of religious and cultural sites, on military matters, on political matters, on legal matters, on demographic matters, and on propaganda matters. They want, under their application, to have essentially an expert-free case presented to the next Trial Chamber. And we submit that that request should be rejected, and it should be rejected because 94 bis is the Article that governs the terms of expert witnesses, and it governs disclosure and when disclosure should be made of expert reports. And the disclosure needs to be established by the Trial Chamber or the Pre-Trial Judge, and in this case, there has been no disclosure date imposed on the Prosecutor in respect of expert reports. Therefore, the Prosecutor is not in breach of this Rule. Now, as a general matter, the identities of the experts have been identified to the Defence, in most cases, long ago. They were identified in the -- in August of 2001 with the filing of the provisional pre-trial brief, and they were again identified by name in the summary of their potential testimony on the 2nd of May when we filed our final pre-trial brief. I undertook at the Status Conference on the 10th of May to inform Your Honours in a memorandum what the status of our experts, who they were and when their reports could be expected, and I filed with Your Honours both on the 24th of May and on -- a complete -- an incomplete report indicating, where possible, I would supplement it, and on the 28th of May, I submitted a supplemental report to Your Honours. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, if I understand your argument, it is this: That any document which you have, for whatever reason, not been in a position to provide now to the Defence, the Chamber should allow it on the basis that there is a provision, either in the Statute or the Rules, for its admission at trial. Isn't that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What I am saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because you have done that in relation to Article 22 and 69, which I believe deal with protected witnesses, although I don't think that's the issue here. Because if you take that approach, then it merely makes a nonsense of the pre-trial procedures. If you look towards -- in anticipation, to the trial and you pick out a basis for admitting it at the trial and use that as the ground now in the pre-trial proceedings as to why we should allow you not to proceed -- not to produce it, it seems to me to render the pre-trial proceedings almost neutered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, let me respond by saying the application of Article 22 and Rule 69 and 75 with witnesses who are not disclosed in the pre-trial brief is an exception. We have listed approximately 400 witnesses in our pre-trial brief. The number of witnesses I'm referring to is exceptionally small, and the procedures, it is our submission, permit for such a case. So I am saying, Your Honour, that under those Rules, it is permissible to not list a witness on the pre-trial brief witness list under exceptional circumstances. But each application is unique, has to stand on its own merits, and obviously, if rejected, those witnesses under such circumstances will be disclosed forthwith to the Defence. That is what I intended to say if I didn't say it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now -- so let me return, if I can, to the situation of the experts. As I said, I have given Your Honours a summary of where we stand in respect of the experts. More specifically as to the Defence submission today, they have complained about the unidentified experts in the area of demographics and propaganda. And yesterday when I met with Mr. Pavich and Mr. Murphy -- Mr. O'Sullivan and Mr. Murphy, I identified our demographics expert, and that is Dr. Ewa Tabeau. I will inform Your Honours that we are in the process of discussing and attempting to finalise the arrangements with a propaganda expert. I'm not in a position to identify that person now until those arrangements have been finalised. But once they are, I will submit a report to Your Honours outlining the same general matters I did in my previous report. So it is our submission, Your Honours, that in respect of the experts, we have not breached any rule that govern the disclosure dates of experts. We are working with great diligence to finalise those particular arrangements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, my final submission on this point is that it is premature to foreclose the Trial Chamber that will hear this case. It is premature to exclude expert witnesses. Now, obviously, the third point that has been dealt with by the Defence in their brief is dealing with the extension of the case to Croatia. It's moot. This issue has been withdrawn by the Defence, I won't comment on it. The last prong of their brief dealt with the exclusion of evidence relating to events after the 31st of December, 1992. And we've set forth our response very clearly in the brief, but to reiterate it, we do not intend to lead crime-base evidence beyond the date -- that occurred beyond the date of the 31st of December, 1992. It is our submission, however, that there is relevant evidence that occurred beyond that date that would bear on the facts and the events that occurred during the time frame of the indictment, and we cited one such example in our brief. We would submit, Your Honour, that the Trial Chamber that is going to hear this case would be the proper Trial Chamber to make determinations as to evidence as it is presented to them, and they should be -- and they will be guided by the provisions of Rule 89. Now, Your Honours, I recognise, I clearly recognise the Trial Chamber's ability and the Trial Chamber's right to take measures that are necessary to cut back on the case, but I would refer Your Honours to a case, a decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Galic case, entitled The Decision on the Application by the Prosecutor for Leave to Appeal. It is dated the 14th of December, 2001. And the facts in that case involved a Pre-Trial Judge of a Trial Chamber that was not going to hear the case excluding a large volume of documents that had not been disclosed to the Defence on a specific date. And part of the reason for the non-disclosure was due to delays of translations of documents which of course, the Appeals Chamber recognised was a constant problem within this institution. We sought to appeal the decision. A three-member panel of the Appeals Chamber denied our application but found that, under the circumstances of the case in Galic, it was unwise for the Trial Chamber that would not hear the case to exclude evidence that would be tendered before a completely new Trial Chamber. It is our submission, Your Honours, that granting the relief in this case sought by the accused would, first, violate the fundamental fairness to the Prosecutor to try their case fully and completely. We believe that the application, if granted, would emasculate the Prosecutor's case and make it essentially a case where the result could be, indeed would be, inevitable. Second of all, Your Honour, we believe it's premature and inappropriate, given the cooperation that the Prosecutors have been engaged in with the Defence and the progress that has been made in respect of translations, we're working well together. The timetable that I've given the Trial Chamber will allow the Defence sufficient time to prepare its pre-trial brief. Lastly, as I mentioned, there are alternatives to the wholesale exclusion of untranslated documents. I have suggested one in my submissions. Therefore, Mr. President, in respect of this motion, I've concluded my remarks. I will say there are other issues I'd like to raise with the Trial Chamber briefly in -- when the occasion presents itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Does anybody want to reply very briefly to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, yes. To emphasise a point that Judge Robinson made as to whether these documents that we're discussing are important, the answer to that is that they certainly are. Many of the untranslated documents, for example, are alleged to be transcripts of telephone -- intercepted telephone conversations to which it is said that Mrs. Plavsic was a party. Obviously of the greatest possible importance. And, Your Honour, at the end of the day, while not disagreeing with Mr. Harmon's submissions about what the Rules say, the overriding question is one of fairness. This is not an experiment in translation projects. We are grateful to Mr. Tieger for his initiative, we will support the Novi Sad project as much as we can, work with him all we can, but at the end of the day, and without being in the least flippant about it, Your Honour, the fact is that the Titanic has struck the iceberg and the Prosecution are suggesting that it's time for the band to strike up Abide With Me, and we cannot get a fair trial without having access to the evidence, and that's really what this motion is about. One must look at the whole picture. The whole picture is that we have a vast amount of evidence, and the statistic that the Prosecution brought forward about the pre-trial brief confirms what we thought, that there are roughly about one-third of the documents in the pre-trial brief that are in B/C/S only. And it cannot really be said -- and I think the Pre-Trial Judge has made it clear that the pre-trial brief is supposed to be a road map, it's supposed to be a trial-ready document, and the fact is that we really can't say that it is while it's in this condition. So issues of fairness, Your Honour, demand this relief that we're seeking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you comment briefly on the reference to the Appeals Chamber's decision in Galic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. As Mr. Harmon pointed out, the Prosecution's application for leave to appeal was denied in that case. There are -- the dicta applied -- this is a very fact specific case. We don't know how many documents there were in Galic or what the exact state of the translation problem was at that time and it may very well be that it was a different case. Your Honour, this case and another case that Your Honours are very familiar with, the Milosevic case, are really cases at a different level in this Tribunal from those that have been tried in the past. In the past, we've had largely senior military officers, camp commanders, war crisis officials and so on. The level of this case, however, is the political level. Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Krajisnik are alleged by the Prosecution to have been leading figures in the SDS, in the Bosnian Serb political structure. These are document cases. It is true that we will have a lot of evidence dealing with witnesses of crimes, of course, but the essence of this case, the thing which will make or break this case either way is the documents. And these are of great -- far greater importance, I would respectfully submit, than in other cases that have been before this Tribunal. So while the observations of the Appeals Chamber in Galic, even though perhaps obiter, are clearly entitled to the greatest possible respect, we have to look at this case on its own merit and this is a very different case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, if there are some matters we want raise -- I should say we will consider this, obviously, and give a written decision probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two matters. One is the issue of the last Status Conference, the issue of translation of films, the translation of films that Mr. Brashich informed Your Honours would be, and Your Honours ordered be accomplished in seven days, I am interested in knowing the status of that. I have not received any copies of transcripts of films.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with that. Mr. Brashich, what's going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was sent by airmail on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Brashich, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I believe on the 23rd or the 24th, they were sent by airmail directly to Mr. Harmon. I sent Mr. Harmon a memorandum to that effect, and I believe I copied Ms. Featherstone on that. Am I correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have received the memorandum but I haven't received the film. That's why I'm bringing it to the Court's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could keep us posted on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd be happy to. The second issue I wanted to bring to Your Honours' attention; at the 10 May Status Conference, I raised the issue of the 92 bis statements that remain unresolved. Out of the original 103, there are approximately 15 of those statements. I just would like to inform Your Honours that I have been engaged in conversations with Mr. Murphy on behalf of the Plavsic team. It appears quite likely that we will reach an agreement on the majority of those statements, and I will keep Your Honours apprised of that. You will receive a memo from us very shortly on the ultimate conclusion of that set of discussions, but by my count, we've agreed on at least ten of them right now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'll ask the Legal Officer to step up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there anything else anybody wants to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will consider the motion and our order in relation to. We will adjourn this matter to a date which will be fixed. At the moment, the timetable remains as directed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 1.36 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: ---  Whereupon the Motion Hearing was adjourned
